The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold without boundary and let $g$ be a smooth
symmetric covariant $2$-tensor field on $M$ such that $g_p$ is nondegenerate at
every $p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-covariant-two-tensor-field]]). Assume
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]).
For this general metric define $\flat_p(v):=g_p(v,\cdot)$,
$\sharp_p:=\flat_p^{-1}$, and
$g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta)$.
Nondegeneracy makes $\flat_p$ injective and hence invertible between the
four-dimensional tangent space and its dual. In a chart, $g^{ab}$ are the
entries of the inverse matrix of $(g_{ab})$. These definitions agree with
[[def-gr-inverse-metric-and-musical-isomorphisms]] in its Lorentzian scope.
Here and below repeated upper/lower indices are summed over $0,1,2,3$.
This holds in particular
when $(M,g,N)$ is a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and $g$ is
its metric ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]). For smooth local vector fields
$X,Y,Z$ put

$$K(X,Y,Z):=X\bigl(g(Y,Z)\bigr)+Y\bigl(g(Z,X)\bigr)-Z\bigl(g(X,Y)\bigr)+g([X,Y],Z)+g([Z,X],Y)-g([Y,Z],X),$$

with brackets as in [[def-lie-bracket-of-smooth-vector-fields]].

**(a) Existence and formulas.** There is exactly one affine connection
$\nabla$ on $M$ ([[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]]) satisfying

$$2g(\nabla_XY,Z)=K(X,Y,Z)\qquad\text{for all smooth local }X,Y,Z .$$

It is torsion-free and $g$-compatible, so it is a metric-selected connection
for $(M,g)$, meaning torsion-free and satisfying
$Xg(Y,Z)=g(\nabla_XY,Z)+g(Y,\nabla_XZ)$ for smooth local fields
(the conditions of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] extended here to
nondegenerate $g$); in every smooth chart its
Christoffel symbols are

$$\Gamma^a{}_{bc}=\tfrac12\,g^{ad}\bigl(\partial_bg_{dc}+\partial_cg_{bd}-\partial_dg_{bc}\bigr),$$

with $g^{ad}$ the inverse-metric components defined above
([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]).

**(b) Uniqueness.** If an affine connection $\nabla'$ on $M$ is torsion-free
and $g$-compatible, then $\nabla'=\nabla$. Consequently the class
$\operatorname{LC}(M,g)$ of metric-selected connections has exactly one
element; it is the **Levi–Civita connection** of $g$.

**(c) Induced derivative on tensor fields.** Let $\nabla^*$ be the dual
connection on $T^*M$ and let the product connection of
[[def-product-connection-on-tensor-and-hom-bundles]] act on
$T^r_sM:=(TM)^{\otimes r}\otimes(T^*M)^{\otimes s}$, for integers $r,s\ge0$,
constructed by [[lem-finite-tensor-products-of-smooth-vector-bundles]]. A
type $(r,s)$ tensor at $p$ is a multilinear map
$(T_p^*M)^r\times(T_pM)^s\to\mathbb R$
([[def-type-r-s-tensor-on-a-finite-dimensional-vector-space]]); a smooth
tensor field is a section with smooth coefficients in each local product
frame. The empty product is the scalar line. Its chart components are
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}=T(dx^{a_1},\ldots,dx^{a_r},\partial_{b_1},\ldots,\partial_{b_s})$,
where $dx^a$ is dual to $\partial_a$. This agrees with
[[def-gr-tensor-fields-and-components]] in the Lorentzian case. Put
$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}:=(\nabla_{\partial_c}T)^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}$.
Then, in every smooth chart, for
every smooth tensor field $T$ of type $(r,s)$,

$$T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s;c}=\partial_cT^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}+\sum_{i=1}^{r}\Gamma^{a_i}{}_{dc}\,T^{a_1\cdots d\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots b_s}-\sum_{j=1}^{s}\Gamma^{d}{}_{b_jc}\,T^{a_1\cdots a_r}{}_{b_1\cdots d\cdots b_s},$$

where the slot marked $d$ replaces the named index; this derivative commutes
with every contraction in the sense of [[def-contraction-of-a-mixed-tensor]],
and it annihilates the metric and the inverse metric:

$$g_{ab;c}=0,\qquad g^{ab}{}_{;c}=0 .$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

derivations.claim: Alternation gives $g(F^\sharp v,w)=F(w,v)=-F(v,w)=-g(v,F^\sharp w)$, so $F^\sharp$ is $g$-skew. By [F1] and the product rule, $$\frac{d}{d\tau}g(U,s)=g(D_\tau U,s)+g(U,D_\tau s)=\alpha\kappa+\alpha\left(a\,g(U,F^\sharp s)+b\,\frac{g(U,U)}{c^2}\kappa\right).$$ Skew-adjointness gives $g(U,F^\sharp s)=-\kappa$, and $g(U,U)=-c^2$; therefore the derivative equals $\alpha(1-a-b)\kappa$.

In any chart along a compact subinterval, the spin equation is a linear system $\dot s=A(\tau)s$ with continuous coefficients: the connection coefficients, $U$, $F$, and $g$ are continuous on the compact curve image. Its right-hand side is locally Lipschitz in $s$, so [F2] gives local existence and uniqueness. The coefficient norm is bounded on each compact chart subinterval, say by $C$; iterating the integral equation gives $\|s(\tau)\|\le \|s(\tau_0)\|\sum_{n\ge0}(C|\tau-\tau_0|)^n/n!=\|s(\tau_0)\|e^{C|\tau-\tau_0|}$. Hence no finite endpoint blow-up occurs there, and finitely many chart subintervals cover any compact part of $I$; uniqueness patches the solutions across chart overlaps.

If $a+b=1$, step 1.1 makes $g(U,s)$ constant, so its zero initial value remains zero. On this constraint, $$\frac12\frac{d}{d\tau}g(s,s)=g(s,D_\tau s)=\alpha\left(a\,g(s,F^\sharp s)+\frac{b}{c^2}g(s,U)\kappa\right)=0,$$ since $F^\sharp$ is skew and $g(s,U)=0$.

At the fixed event in the Statement, $s\in E_\tau$ has $s=\sum_js^je_j$. The projection kills the term proportional to $U$, and for each spatial basis vector $e_i$, $g(F^\sharp(s),e_i)=F(e_i,s)=F_{ij}s^j=\epsilon_{ijk}B_ks^j=(\mathbf s\times\mathbf B)_i$. Thus the projected covariant derivative has coefficient $\alpha a$; for $\alpha\ne0$, matching for every $\mathbf s,\mathbf B$ forces $a=G$, and preservation for all initially orthogonal data and alternating fields gives $a+b=1$ by step 1.1, hence $b=1-G$. When $\alpha=0$, the matching condition does not identify the coefficients.

The component formula of [F2] expands to
$$|x\times y|^2=|x|^2|y|^2-(x\cdot y)^2\le|x|^2|y|^2.$$
For almost every $x$ in the support ball, $|x|\le\ell$ and $|j(x)|\le e(x)/c$, so $|x\times j(x)|\le\ell e(x)/c$. From $e,j\in L^1$ in [F3], monotonicity and homogeneity in [F4] give $\int|x\times j|\,d^3x\le\ell E_0/c<\infty$, establishing absolute integrability of $\mathbf s_*$.

If $\mathbf s_*=0$ the bound is immediate. Otherwise set $u=\mathbf s_*/|\mathbf s_*|$, so $|u|=1$. Linearity, the integral triangle inequality [F4] and Cauchy–Schwarz [F5] give
$$|\mathbf s_*|=u\cdot\mathbf s_*=\int u\cdot(x\times j(x))\,d^3x\le\int|u\cdot(x\times j(x))|\,d^3x\le\int|x\times j(x)|\,d^3x\le\frac{\ell E_0}{c}=\ell Mc.$$
This proves the first inequality.
Since $M=E_0/c^2>0$ and $c>0$, divide the inequality of step 2.1 by $Mc$ to obtain $\ell\ge|\mathbf s_*|/(Mc)$.

For a measure $\mu$, write
$$L^1(\mu):=\{f:X\to\mathbb C:\ f \text{ is integrable}\}.$$
Here **integrable** is the notion introduced in
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]].

On this page $L^1(\mu)$ is the class of integrable representatives. The later
Banach-space page will pass to almost-everywhere equivalence classes.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be **bounded**
([[def-bounded-set]]), so that there is a real $M \ge 0$ with $|f(x)| \le M$ for
every $x \in [a,b]$, and let $P = (n,t)$ be a partition of $[a,b]$ with
subintervals $I_i = [t_i, t_{i+1}]$ and lengths $\Delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i$ for
$i < n$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

### The two extreme values on a subinterval

For $i < n$ put

$$m_i \;:=\; \inf f[I_i], \qquad M_i \;:=\; \sup f[I_i], \qquad f[I_i] \;=\; \{\, f(x) : x \in I_i \,\} .$$

**Both exist.** The set $f[I_i]$ is nonempty, because $t_i < t_{i+1}$ makes $I_i$
nonempty ([[def-interval]]), and it is bounded, because $|f(x)| \le M$ for every
$x$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). A nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]); each is unique, so the notations
$\inf f[I_i]$ and $\sup f[I_i]$ name single real numbers ([[lem-sup-unique]]).

**They bracket the values, and each other.** For $x \in I_i$,

$$-M \;\le\; m_i \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M_i \;\le\; M ,$$

the outer inequalities because $-M$ is a lower bound and $M$ an upper bound of
$f[I_i]$, and the middle ones by the definitions of infimum and supremum. In
particular $m_i \le M_i$ and $M_i - m_i \le 2M$.

The dependence of $m_i$ and $M_i$ on $f$ and on $P$ is suppressed in the
notation, as is customary; where two partitions are in play the sums below carry
the partition and the extreme values are written out.

### The two Darboux sums

$$L(f,P) \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} m_i \,\Delta_i, \qquad U(f,P) \;:=\; \sum_{i<n} M_i \,\Delta_i ,$$

the finite sums of [[def-finite-sum]], indexed by $i \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$i < n$. Both are real numbers, being finite sums of reals, and

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

by monotonicity of finite sums, clause 4 of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]], since
$m_i \Delta_i \le M_i \Delta_i$ for every $i < n$: multiplying $m_i \le M_i$ by
$\Delta_i > 0$ preserves the inequality ([[def-ordered-field]]).

### The gap on a subinterval is the oscillation there

For every $i < n$,

$$M_i - m_i \;=\; \omega_f(I_i) \;=\; \sup\{\, |f(x) - f(y)| \ : \ x, y \in I_i \,\} ,$$

the oscillation of $f$ on the set $I_i$ ([[def-oscillation]]). The supremum is a
real number here rather than an extended one, because $f$ is bounded
([[def-oscillation]], [[def-extended-reals]]). The identity is proved in two
inequalities.

*The oscillation is at most the gap.* For $x, y \in I_i$ both $f(x)$ and $f(y)$
lie in $[m_i, M_i]$, so $f(x) - f(y) \le M_i - m_i$ and
$f(y) - f(x) \le M_i - m_i$, whence $|f(x) - f(y)| \le M_i - m_i$
([[lem-of-abs-value]]). So $M_i - m_i$ is an upper bound of the set whose
supremum is $\omega_f(I_i)$.

*The gap is at most the oscillation.* Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be real. By the
$\varepsilon$-characterisations of the supremum and the infimum
([[lem-sup-epsilon]], [[lem-inf-epsilon]]) there are $x, y \in I_i$ with
$f(x) > M_i - \varepsilon/2$ and $f(y) < m_i + \varepsilon/2$; then

$$|f(x) - f(y)| \;\ge\; f(x) - f(y) \;>\; (M_i - m_i) - \varepsilon ,$$

so $\omega_f(I_i) > (M_i - m_i) - \varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon > 0$ was
arbitrary, $\omega_f(I_i) \ge M_i - m_i$: otherwise
$\varepsilon := (M_i - m_i) - \omega_f(I_i)$ would be positive and give
$\omega_f(I_i) > \omega_f(I_i)$.

This identity is what connects the Darboux machinery to the pointwise
oscillation of [[def-oscillation]], and it is the hinge of
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

derivations.claim: For each component $k$, write $D^2b_k(x)[u,v]=\sum_{i,j=1}^3 a_{ij}(x)u_iv_j$. The coefficients $a_{ij}$ are continuous because $b$ is $C^2$. The ball is compact by [F3], so the finitely many coefficients have a common bound $C_k<\infty$ there. Since $|u_i|\le|u|$ and $|v_j|\le|v|$, the sum has magnitude at most $9C_k|u||v|$, hence the displayed bilinear supremum and $M_k$ are finite. For nonzero $u,v$, apply that supremum to $u/|u|,v/|v|$ and multiply by $|u||v|$; when either vector is zero the bilinear expression is zero. This proves the homogeneous bound used below. Since $|y-z|\le\ell$ on the support, monotonicity and homogeneity in [F2] show that each moment is absolutely integrable: $|Q|\le\|\rho\|_1$ and $|d_i|\le\ell\|\rho\|_1$. By compactness of the ball and continuity of each $b_k$, [F3] bounds $b_k$ there, so $\rho b_k$ is integrable as well.

Fix $y\in\overline B_\ell(z)$ and component $k$, and set $\phi(t)=b_k(z+t(y-z))$ on $[0,1]$. The segment stays in the closed ball, and the chain rule [F4] gives $\phi'(0)=Db_k(z)(y-z)$ and $\phi''(t)=D^2b_k(z+t(y-z))[y-z,y-z]$, hence $|\phi''(t)|\le C:=M_k|y-z|^2$. Set $H(t)=(1-t)\phi'(t)+\phi(t)$ and $f(t):=H'(t)=(1-t)\phi''(t)$. This derivative is continuous and Riemann integrable by [F3], so [F4] gives $r_k(y):=b_k(y)-b_k(z)-Db_k(z)(y-z)=\int_0^1 f(t)\,dt$. To bound this Riemann integral, let $h_\pm(t):=\pm C(1-t)$. The pointwise inequalities $h_-\le f\le h_+$ imply $L(h_-,P)\le L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P)\le U(h_+,P)$ for every partition, by the infimum, supremum and positive weights in [F6]. Taking the corresponding supremum and infimum gives $\int h_-\le\int f\le\int h_+$. The continuous functions $h_\pm$ have primitives $\pm C(t-t^2/2)$, so [F4] evaluates their integrals as $\pm C/2$. Consequently $|r_k(y)|\le\tfrac12M_k|y-z|^2$.

The function $r_k$ defined in step 2.1 is continuous on the ball. Its bound there makes $\rho r_k$ absolutely Lebesgue integrable by [F2]. Multiply that component expansion by $\rho(y)$ and integrate over $\overline B_\ell(z)$. Linearity [F1] gives $\mathcal B_k=Qb_k(z)+Db_k(z)d+R_k$, with $R_k=\int_{\overline B_\ell(z)}\rho(y)r_k(y)\,d^3y$. By the Lebesgue integral triangle inequality and domination [F2], $|R_k|\le\tfrac12M_k\ell^2\int_{\overline B_\ell(z)}|\rho|\,d^3y\le\tfrac12M_k\ell^2\|\rho\|_1$.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$
   ([[def-affine-space-and-displacement]]). In particular $V$ is a real vector
   space of dimension $4$.
2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of
   inertia $(3,1,0)$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]). Its associated quadratic
   form is $q(v)=\eta(v,v)$.
3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

They are primitive model parameters; this definition does not derive them from the background field or from another framework.
- The **kinetic four-momentum** is the derived vector $P:=mU$ along $z$, with unit kilogram metre per second.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure, and let $\nabla$ be the metric-selected Levi–Civita connection of [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]. Let $U$ and the prescribed external two-form $F$ be as in [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], and let the translational motion obey the adopted action law [[post-rpm-external-charge-action]]. For a $C^1$ spin or polarization vector $s$ along the worldline with $g(s,U)=0$, define $G:=g_s/2$ and $K:=F(s,U)=g(s,F^\sharp(U))$. Adopt the transport law

(a) [Components] For a field pair $(E,B)$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, define the
covariant components of the **electromagnetic two-form** $F$ in the chart by
$F_{00}=0$, $F_{0i}:=-E_i/c$, $F_{ij}:=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$
($i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$) and $F_{ab}:=-F_{ba}$, the index-raised components being
$F^{0i}=E_i/c$, $F^{i0}=-E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Here
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the spatial permutation symbol of
[[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]. Then $F$ is a $C^k$ type-$(0,2)$
tensor field on $U$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], alternating at every event, and the
components above are exactly its component functions: at $p\in U$ the tensor
$F(p)$ is the bilinear form $F(p)(u,w)=F_{ab}(p)u^aw^b$ on $V$ in the
coordinates $u^a,w^b$ of $u,w$ in $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. Indeed each $F_{ab}$ is
a finite sum of products of the $C^k$ functions $E_i,B_k$ of the chart
coordinates with the constants $c,\epsilon_{ijk}$, hence a $C^k$ function of
$x(p)$, and the component criterion of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]] applies.

It is distinct from the potential-dependent covector defined in [[lem-rpm-charge-gauge-boundary]].
- The **spin or polarization vector** is a $C^1$ tangent vector field $s(\tau)\in T_{z(\tau)}M$ constrained by $g(s,U)=0$, so it lies in the positive-definite instantaneous rest space $U^\perp$.

Assume Countable Choice for the canonical tangent-bundle smooth structure supplied by the GR items below. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold with its metric-compatible connection $\nabla$, let $c>0$, and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval of proper-time values. Let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve and set $U:=dz/d\tau$, with $g(U,U)=-c^2$. For a $C^1$ vector field $V$ along $z$, define its covariant derivative by the pullback connection $D_\tau V:=(z^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial\tau}V$; in a chart this means $(D_\tau V)^a=dV^a/d\tau+\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(z(\tau))U^bV^c$. Let $F_\tau$ be a continuous alternating two-form along $z$. Define $F^\sharp_\tau$ by
$$g(F^\sharp_\tau(v),w)=F_\tau(w,v).$$
Then $F^\sharp_\tau$ is skew-adjoint with respect to $g$.

For constants $\alpha,a,b\in\mathbb R$, consider a $C^1$ vector field $s$ along $z$ satisfying the restricted linear transport equations
$$D_\tau U=\alpha F^\sharp(U),\qquad D_\tau s=\alpha\left(aF^\sharp(s)+\frac{b}{c^2}U\,\kappa\right),\qquad \kappa:=g(s,F^\sharp(U)).$$
For every $\tau_0\in I$ and initial value $s(\tau_0)$ there is a unique solution on each compact subinterval of $I$ containing $\tau_0$. Along any such solution,
$$\frac{d}{d\tau}g(U,s)=\alpha(1-a-b)\kappa.$$
Consequently, the orthogonality constraint $g(U,s)=0$ is preserved when $a+b=1$, and on that constraint $g(s,s)$ is constant. For the coefficient comparison, fix a parameter value $\tau$ and put $n:=U(\tau)/c$. Then $n$ is an observer at $z(\tau)$ and its rest space is the three-dimensional positive-definite subspace $E_\tau:=n^\perp=U(\tau)^\perp$ (the observer and projection conventions are those of [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]] and [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]). Choose an orientation of $E_\tau$ and a positively oriented orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; set $e_0:=n$. For $v\in E_\tau$, write $\mathbf v=(g(v,e_1),g(v,e_2),g(v,e_3))$, use $(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}u_jv_k$, and define $\mathbf B$ by $F_{ij}:=F(e_i,e_j)=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. Let $P_U(v):=v+g(U,v)U/c^2$, the projection onto $E_\tau$, and fix a target coefficient $G\in\mathbb R$. The rest-space matching condition means the pointwise equality
$$\bigl(P_U(D_\tau s)\bigr)^i=\alpha G\,(\mathbf s\times\mathbf B)_i\qquad(i=1,2,3)$$
for every $\mathbf s,\mathbf B\in\mathbb R^3$, when $s(\tau)\in E_\tau$. Thus it compares spatial components of the covariant derivative at the event, not the derivative of components in an unspecified moving tetrad. For $\alpha\ne0$, if the coefficients both preserve $g(U,s)=0$ for every initially orthogonal datum and every allowed alternating field and satisfy this matching condition, then $a=G$ and $b=1-G$. Conversely, these coefficients satisfy both requirements. This uniqueness is only within the displayed two-term ansatz; no uniqueness among all covariant spin-transport laws is asserted. If $\alpha=0$, the rest-space matching condition does not identify $a$ or $b$.

1. A nonempty affine space $A$ over a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$,
   with action $(p,v)\mapsto p+v$ and displacement $q-p\in V$

2. A Lorentz form $\eta$ on $V$, i.e. a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form of

3. An **orientation** of $V$: a positive ray of the determinant line
   $\Lambda^4V$, fixed once and for all
   ([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).
4. A **time orientation** $C^+$ of $(V,\eta)$: one of the two connected
   components of the timelike set $T=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$, the other being
   $C^-:=T\setminus C^+$ ([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]).

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with time orientation
$C^+$ ([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]] is the form;
[[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]] fixes $C^+$), and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), with spatial three-space $S$ and
Euclidean form $\delta$. Then:

Fix $c>0$ and a future unit observer $n$ in an affine Minkowski spacetime as in [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. Identify the positive-definite rest space $n^\perp$ isometrically with $\mathbb R^3$, with its Euclidean norm $|\cdot|$ and Lebesgue measure $d^3x$. Define the closed Euclidean ball by
$$\overline B_\ell(0):=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x|\le\ell\}.$$
Let $e:\mathbb R^3\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable with $e\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$, and let $j:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be measurable with each component $j_i\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ for $i=1,2,3$. Thus $j$ is vector-valued integrable and every vector integral below is the componentwise Lebesgue integral. Assume $e$ and $j$ are both zero almost everywhere outside $\overline B_\ell(0)$ for some $\ell>0$, and that $|j(x)|\le e(x)/c$ almost everywhere. Define
$$E_0:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}e(x)\,d^3x>0,\qquad M:=E_0/c^2,\qquad \mathbf s_*:=\int_{\mathbb R^3}x\times j(x)\,d^3x.$$
Then $\mathbf s_*$ is absolutely integrable and
$$|\mathbf s_*|\le\ell Mc,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \ell\ge\frac{|\mathbf s_*|}{Mc}.$$
The hypotheses are the full mathematical content of this estimate; it is not a bound for a quantum point particle or for a source whose energy density or momentum density fails them.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski space, with signature $(-+++)$, and fix $c>0$. Let $p$ be any future timelike vector and define $M:=\sqrt{-\eta(p,p)}/c>0$. Choose an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] with $e_0=p/(Mc)$, so its ordered orthonormal basis is future and positively oriented and $p$ has components $(Mc,\mathbf 0)$ in this frame. Its positive-definite rest space is $e_0^\perp=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; use $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ for spatial components and the induced right-handed symbol $\epsilon_{ijk}$. Let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ satisfy the momentum supplementary condition $S^{ab}p_b=0$, and set $s_*^k:=\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}S^{ij}$ in this oriented orthonormal rest-space basis. Every future unit observer has the components
$$n=\gamma\left(e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3\frac{v^i}{c}e_i\right),\qquad \gamma=(1-|\mathbf v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2},\qquad |\mathbf v|<c,$$
by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. For every such observer, define
$$\delta^a:=\frac{S^{ab}n_b}{p\cdot n},\qquad S'^{ab}:=S^{ab}-(\delta^ap^b-\delta^bp^a).$$
Then $p\cdot n\ne0$, $\delta\cdot p=\delta\cdot n=0$, and $S'^{ab}n_b=0$. Let $z\in A$ be the representative event. For $u,v\in V$, define $(u\wedge v)^{ab}:=u^av^b-u^bv^a$. If the representative point changes by $z\mapsto z+\delta$, the total angular momentum about the frame origin $o$,
$$J_o:=(z-o)\wedge p+S,$$
is unchanged by this stipulated spin-shift rule. In the rest space,
$$\boldsymbol\delta=\frac{\mathbf s_*\times\mathbf v}{Mc^2},$$
If $\mathbf s_*\ne0$, the shifts of all future timelike observers fill the open disk in $\mathbf s_*^\perp$ of radius $|\mathbf s_*|/(Mc)$; the boundary is a supremum and is not attained. If $\mathbf s_*=0$, only the zero shift occurs. This is an exact affine-flat algebraic result.

For a finite $C^2$ future-timelike curve segment $z:[a,b]\to O$ in that domain, where $a<b$ are proper-time endpoints, and the local $C^2$ fixed-endpoint variations of the postulate, choose the orientation-preserving parameter $\lambda=\tau$; the segment is stationary for the adopted action if and only if

$$m\nabla_UU=qF^\sharp(U),\qquad (\nabla_UU)_a=\frac qm F_{ab}U^b.$$

This is a model deduction: it establishes the equation equivalent to stationarity of the postulated functional, not the physical truth of the postulate.

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. For a neutral test body, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of proper-time values and let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve, with $U=dz/d\tau$. Let $p^a$ and $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be the momentum and spin moments of [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. For a $C^1$ vector or rank-two tensor field $V$ along $z$, define $D_\tau V:=(z^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial\tau}V$ using the pullback of the metric-selected connection. In a chart, with $\Gamma$ the coefficients of $\nabla$, this is
$$
(D_\tau p)^a=\frac{dp^a}{d\tau}+\Gamma^a{}_{bc}U^bp^c,\qquad (D_\tau S)^{ab}=\frac{dS^{ab}}{d\tau}+\Gamma^a{}_{cd}U^cS^{db}+\Gamma^b{}_{cd}U^cS^{ad}.
$$
Adopt the pole-dipole evolution equations
$$D_\tau p^a=-\frac12 R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd},\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a.$$
A spin-supplementary condition (SSC) is an additional equation $S^{ab}n_b=0$ for a specified future unit timelike field $n$ along $z$; this postulate does not select one SSC, and $p$ is an independently evolved moment rather than a primitive assumption $p=mU$.

For a chosen finite multipole model, let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_r\to M$ be the declared tensor bundles of its additional moments. Its state bundle is the fiber product over $M$ of $TM$ for $U$, $TM$ for $p$, $\Lambda^2TM$ for $S$, and the bundles $Q_1,\ldots,Q_r$, restricted to states with $U$ future timelike and $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and to the stated algebraic constraints on the moments. Fix an open admissible state domain $\mathcal D$ in this bundle. The extra force and torque are specified smooth bundle maps over the identity, $f_{\rm extra}:\mathcal D\to TM$ and $N_{\rm extra}:\mathcal D\to\Lambda^2TM$, so at a state based at $x\in M$ their values lie in $T_xM$ and $\Lambda^2T_xM$, respectively. Their units are $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$. For a retained quadrupole or higher-multipole model, adopt
$$D_\tau p^a=-\frac12 R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd}+f_{\rm extra}^a,\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a+N_{\rm extra}^{ab},$$
where $f_{\rm extra}$ is a specified smooth force map along the state and $N_{\rm extra}^{ab}=-N_{\rm extra}^{ba}$ is a specified smooth torque map. A quadrupole convention that may be adopted is
$$f_{\rm quad}^a=-\frac16J^{bcde}\nabla^aR_{bcde},\qquad N_{\rm quad}^{ab}=\frac43R^{[a}{}_{cde}J^{b]cde},$$
with $J^{bcde}$ satisfying the algebraic symmetries of the curvature tensor, carrying units $\mathrm{kg\,m^4\,s^{-2}}$, and brackets including the factor $1/2$. Any evolved $J$ or higher moment needs its own transport or constitutive law; without it the multipole equations are not a closed initial-value model.

The pole-dipole and multipole equations are adopted finite-dimensional truncations, not derivations from the moment integrals above. Their use as approximations for a material body is restricted to regimes in which its size is small compared with the relevant curvature and background-variation lengths and omitted moment effects are negligible on the stated finite interval. These conditions are qualitative applicability assumptions here: this postulate supplies no uniform error bound, no convergence of truncations, and no global existence claim. No experimental result or measurement is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice and use a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,N)$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ with its metric-compatible Levi–Civita connection. Use SI units: coordinates are metres, proper time is seconds, $c>0$ is in metres per second, $p$ is in kilogram metres per second, $S$ is in kilogram metres squared per second, and $R$ has inverse-square-metre components. Let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline parametrized by proper time, with $U=dz/d\tau$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. For $C^1$ tensor fields along this $C^2$ curve, use the chart-independent derivative defined in [[lem-rpm-ssc-momentum-identity]]: differentiate the components, add $+\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(z)U^b$ on each upper index, and add $-\Gamma^c{}_{ba}(z)U^b$ on each lower index. It obeys the product and contraction rules and $D_\tau g=0$, as proved there. Let $p$ be a $C^1$ future timelike vector field along $z$, let $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be a $C^1$ bivector field, and suppose the displayed evolution equations hold:

$$D_\tau p^a=f^a:=-\frac12R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd},\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a.\tag{1}$$

Put $\mu:=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}>0$, $m:=-g(p,U)/c^2>0$, $C^a:=S^{ab}p_b$, and define the linear map

$$K^a{}_b:=\mu^2\delta^a_b-\frac12S^{ac}R_{cbde}S^{de}.$$

At every state where $K$ is invertible and $W:=K^{-1}p$ is future timelike, the TD condition $C=0$ and (1) imply

$$KU=mc^2p,\qquad U=\frac{cW}{\sqrt{-g(W,W)}}.\tag{2}$$

Conversely, on the open state region where $p$ and $W$ are future timelike and $K$ is invertible, the normalized formula for $U$ in (2), together with (1), defines a smooth local ODE. A solution initialized with $C=0$ preserves $C=0$. While it remains in that admissible region, $\mu$ and $S_{ab}S^{ab}/2$ are constant. If $S=0$, then $p=(\mu/c)U$, $D_\tau p=0$, and $D_\tau U=0$. These are local statements; no continuation past loss of invertibility of $K$ or timelikeness of $W$ is asserted. Equations (1) are hypotheses of this mathematical lemma, not a physical derivation of a stress-energy moment model.

Use the charged/spinning body-model conventions of the now-authored batch-24 carrier [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]: a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-+++)$, coordinates $x^0=ct$ in metres, $c>0$, and a $C^2$ future timelike representative curve $\zeta:I\to M$ parametrized by proper time $\tau$ in seconds, with $U=d\zeta/d\tau$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. The actual supplier defines these quantities and the SI electromagnetic-tensor convention used here. Assume Countable Choice for the GR smooth-structure, convex-normal and parallel-transport suppliers used below.

**(a) Flat isolated-body moments.** Choose an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], with the SI coordinate convention $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]. Thus $e_0$ is future unit timelike and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the positively oriented orthonormal spatial basis. Let $T$ be a $C^\infty$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field on the affine Minkowski spacetime $A$, whose chart components $T^{ab}$ are the model stress-energy densities with units $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$. The coordinate-time image $J:=\{x^0(\zeta(\tau))/c:\tau\in I\}$ is an open interval, and $\zeta(t)$ denotes the unique point of the curve with coordinate time $t$; this is well-defined because future timelike curves have strictly increasing inertial coordinate time. For a finite closed interval $[t_1,t_2]\subset\mathbb R$, define
$$K_{[t_1,t_2]}:=\overline{\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:\text{there are }t\in[t_1,t_2]\text{ and }a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}\text{ with }T^{ab}(ct,\mathbf x)\ne0\}}.$$
Assume $K_{[t_1,t_2]}$ is compact for every such interval. For each $t\in\mathbb R$, define the spatial support by
$$\operatorname{supp}_tT:=\overline{\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:\text{there are }a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}\text{ with }T^{ab}(ct,\mathbf x)\ne0\}}.$$
At a fixed time $t$, the spatial slice has coordinates $\mathbf x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^3$ and three-dimensional Lebesgue measure $d^3x$; define
$$p^a(t):=\frac1c\int_{\mathbb R^3}T^{0a}(ct,\mathbf x)\,d^3x,$$
and, for the representative event $\zeta(t)$ on that time slice, define
$$S_{\zeta(t)}^{ab}(t):=\frac1c\int_{\mathbb R^3}\left((x-\zeta(t))^aT^{0b}(ct,\mathbf x)-(x-\zeta(t))^bT^{0a}(ct,\mathbf x)\right)d^3x.$$
Here $(x-\zeta(t))^0=0$ on the chosen slice, $p$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_{\zeta(t)}$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. These are definitions of moments; no conservation is asserted by clause (a).

**(b) Local curved-body moments.** Let $z\in M$ and let $U_0$ be a convex normal neighborhood containing $z$. Let $\Sigma=i(S)\subset U_0$ be a $C^1$ embedded spacelike hypersurface through $z$, where $S$ is a three-dimensional $C^1$ manifold without boundary and $i:S\to U_0$ is an injective $C^1$ immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image. Thus each tangent space $T_x\Sigma$ is three-dimensional; require the restriction of $g_x$ to it to be positive definite. Let $n_x$ be its continuous future unit normal, meaning $g_x(n_x,n_x)=-1$ and $g_x(n_x,w)=0$ for every $w\in T_x\Sigma$. For a local parametrization $X:V\subseteq\mathbb R^3\to\Sigma$, put $g^\Sigma_{ij}(y):=g_{X(y)}(\partial_iX,\partial_jX)$ and define
$$d\Sigma:=\sqrt{\det(g^\Sigma_{ij}(y))}\,dy^1dy^2dy^3.$$
The positive-definite condition makes this density positive, and the coordinate-change rule makes the resulting measure independent of the parametrization; $dy^1dy^2dy^3$ is Lebesgue measure on $V$. Let $T$ be a smooth symmetric type-$(2,0)$ stress-energy tensor field on $U_0$, with components in an orthonormal tetrad in joules per cubic metre; only its restriction $T|_\Sigma$ is used. With $(n_x)_b:=g_{bc}(x)n_x^c$, define
$$\operatorname{supp}_\Sigma(T|_\Sigma):=\overline{\{x\in\Sigma:T_x\ne0\}}^{\,\Sigma}.$$
Assume this restricted support is a compact subset of $U_0$ and that all displayed integrands are absolutely integrable with respect to $d\Sigma$. For every $x\in\Sigma$, let $v(x):=\exp_z^{-1}(x)\in T_zM$ be the unique joining position vector supplied by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]] and [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $H_{x\to z}:T_xM\to T_zM$ be parallel transport along that unique geodesic, with existence, uniqueness and metric preservation as in [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]]. Define $T^\sharp(n_x)^a:=T^{ab}(x)(n_x)_b$ and
$$p_z:=\frac1c\int_\Sigma H_{x\to z}\!\left(-T^\sharp(n_x)\right)d\Sigma,\qquad S_z:=\frac1c\int_\Sigma v(x)\wedge H_{x\to z}\!\left(-T^\sharp(n_x)\right)d\Sigma,$$
where $(v\wedge w)^{ab}:=v^aw^b-v^bw^a$ and the finite-dimensional vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise in any basis of $T_zM$. The resulting $p_z$ and $S_z$ are a vector and an antisymmetric tensor at $z$; their units are $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. “Support on $\Sigma$” here means only compact support of the restriction $T|_\Sigma$; it does not assert that the ambient smooth field $T$ has spacetime support contained in $\Sigma$.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold and let
$p\in M$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]).

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector
$n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of
[[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$. Because
$g_p(n,n)=-1\neq0$, an observer is timelike and in particular nonzero
([[def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors]]). Observers at $p$ exist:
the vector $N_p$ is timelike, and
$n:=N_p/\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}$ satisfies $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and
$g_p(n,N_p)=-\sqrt{-g_p(N_p,N_p)}<0$, where the square root is the
nonnegative root of [[def-rational-power]]; then $-n$ is a unit timelike
vector with $g_p(-n,N_p)>0$, so it is not an observer, and the two vectors
$n,-n$ point in opposite time directions.

**(b) Rest space.** For an observer $n$ at $p$, the **rest space** of $n$ is
the $g_p$-orthogonal complement of the line $\mathbb Rn$,

$$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM: g_p(v,n)=0\},$$

in the sense of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. It is
a linear subspace of $T_pM$. The further facts that $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and
that the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite are proved
in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]]; they are consequences, not
part of the definition.

**(c) Spatial projection.** The **spatial projection** of the observer $n$ is
the map

$$h_n:T_pM\longrightarrow T_pM,\qquad h_n(v):=v+g_p(n,v)\,n .$$

The map is linear because $g_p$ is bilinear, its image is contained in
$n^{\perp}$, and it fixes $n^{\perp}$ pointwise; that it is the
$g_p$-orthogonal projection onto $n^{\perp}$ with kernel $\mathbb Rn$ is
proved in [[lem-gr-observer-projection-decomposition]].

**(d) Scope.** An observer at $p$ is a single tangent vector. It is not an
ordered basis or frame of $T_pM$, not a chart, not a field of observers such as
the congruences defined later on this page, and not a curve or a worldline: no
parametrized curve, clock reading, proper time or measurement is attached to
$n$ by this definition. The physical reading of an observer as the direction
of an ideal clock's worldline, and the measurement interpretation of the
observer-relative quantities introduced later on this page, belong to the
physical postulates and unit conventions of the framework and are not asserted
here.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold, let
$p\in M$, and let $n$ be an observer at $p$
([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]). Write $h:=h_n$,
$n^{\perp}=\{v\in T_pM:g_p(v,n)=0\}$
([[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]) and
$\mathbb Rn=\{\lambda n:\lambda\in\mathbb R\}$. Then:

1. $h:T_pM\to T_pM$ is linear, $h(n)=0$, $h(v)=v$ for every $v\in n^{\perp}$
   and $h\circ h=h$; its kernel is $\ker h=\mathbb Rn$, its image is
   $\operatorname{im}h=n^{\perp}$, and
   $T_pM=\mathbb Rn\oplus n^{\perp}$ is an orthogonal direct sum: every
   $v\in T_pM$ has the unique decomposition

   $$v=-g_p(v,n)\,n+h(v),$$

   in which $-g_p(v,n)n\in\mathbb Rn$ and $h(v)\in n^{\perp}$.
2. For all $v,w\in T_pM$ the **projection identity**

   $$g_p(h(v),h(w))=g_p(v,w)+g_p(v,n)g_p(n,w)$$

   holds; in particular $g_p(h(v),h(v))=g_p(v,v)+g_p(v,n)^2$.
3. $\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive
   definite.

Suppose also $S(\tau_0)=0$. Step 1.1 preserves $C^a=S^{ab}p_b=0$ and the scalar $\frac12S_{ab}S^{ab}$, while the admissible region keeps $p$ future timelike. At each $\tau$, set $\mu=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}>0$, $e_0=p/\mu$, and $E:=e_0^\perp$; [F3] says $E$ is a three-dimensional positive-definite inner-product space. Take any basis $v_1,v_2,v_3$ of $E$ and form
$$e_1:=\frac{v_1}{\sqrt{g(v_1,v_1)}},\quad w_2:=v_2-g(v_2,e_1)e_1,\quad e_2:=\frac{w_2}{\sqrt{g(w_2,w_2)}},\quad w_3:=v_3-g(v_3,e_1)e_1-g(v_3,e_2)e_2,\quad e_3:=\frac{w_3}{\sqrt{g(w_3,w_3)}}.$$
The denominators are positive: positive definiteness gives $g(v_1,v_1)>0$, and linear independence of the $v_i$ makes $w_2,w_3$ nonzero. These formulas give an orthonormal basis of $E$; with $e_0$ they give an orthonormal basis of $T_{z(\tau)}M$. The TD constraint says $S^{ab}p_b=0$; since $p_b=(-\mu,0,0,0)$ in this basis, it gives $S^{a0}=0$, and antisymmetry also gives $S^{0a}=0$. Therefore
$$\frac12S_{ab}S^{ab}=\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^3(S^{ij})^2\ge0,$$
with equality if and only if every component $S^{ij}$ vanishes, that is, $S=0$. Its conserved value is initially zero, so $S$ remains zero throughout the local solution. The zero-spin branch in [F1] now yields $p=(\mu/c)U$ and $D_\tau p=0$. Since [F1] also gives constant $\mu>0$, covariant differentiation of $U=(c/\mu)p$ gives $D_\tau U=0$. Therefore $z$ is a timelike geodesic in proper-time parametrization and $M=\mu/c$ is constant. No continuation outside the admissible region is supplied.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

$$D_\tau U=\alpha F^\sharp(U),\qquad D_\tau s=\alpha\left[GF^\sharp(s)-(G-1)\frac{U}{c^2}g(s,F^\sharp(U))\right],\qquad g(U,U)=-c^2,\quad g(U,s)=0.$$
The tensor equation is covariant under proper orthochronous Lorentz transformations of the complete field and worldline data. If $F=0$, then $D_\tau U=0$ and $D_\tau s=0$. For any acceleration $a=D_\tau U$ within the Lorentz-force model, the $G=0$ branch is Fermi–Walker transport on the orthogonal spin subspace:
$$D_\tau s=\frac{1}{c^2}\bigl(Ug(a,s)-a g(U,s)\bigr)=\frac{U}{c^2}g(a,s).$$

Assume Countable Choice as inherited from [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. For a neutral test body, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval of proper-time values and let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve, with $U=dz/d\tau$. Let $p^a$ and $S^{ab}=-S^{ba}$ be the momentum and spin moments of [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. For a $C^1$ vector or rank-two tensor field $V$ along $z$, define $D_\tau V:=(z^*\nabla)_{\partial/\partial\tau}V$ using the pullback of the metric-selected connection. In a chart, with $\Gamma$ the coefficients of $\nabla$, this is
$$
(D_\tau p)^a=\frac{dp^a}{d\tau}+\Gamma^a{}_{bc}U^bp^c,\qquad (D_\tau S)^{ab}=\frac{dS^{ab}}{d\tau}+\Gamma^a{}_{cd}U^cS^{db}+\Gamma^b{}_{cd}U^cS^{ad}.
$$
Adopt the pole-dipole evolution equations
$$D_\tau p^a=-\frac12 R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd},\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a.$$
A spin-supplementary condition (SSC) is an additional equation $S^{ab}n_b=0$ for a specified future unit timelike field $n$ along $z$; this postulate does not select one SSC, and $p$ is an independently evolved moment rather than a primitive assumption $p=mU$.

For a chosen finite multipole model, let $Q_1,\ldots,Q_r\to M$ be the declared tensor bundles of its additional moments. Its state bundle is the fiber product over $M$ of $TM$ for $U$, $TM$ for $p$, $\Lambda^2TM$ for $S$, and the bundles $Q_1,\ldots,Q_r$, restricted to states with $U$ future timelike and $g(U,U)=-c^2$ and to the stated algebraic constraints on the moments. Fix an open admissible state domain $\mathcal D$ in this bundle. The extra force and torque are specified smooth bundle maps over the identity, $f_{\rm extra}:\mathcal D\to TM$ and $N_{\rm extra}:\mathcal D\to\Lambda^2TM$, so at a state based at $x\in M$ their values lie in $T_xM$ and $\Lambda^2T_xM$, respectively. Their units are $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-2}}$. For a retained quadrupole or higher-multipole model, adopt
$$D_\tau p^a=-\frac12 R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd}+f_{\rm extra}^a,\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a+N_{\rm extra}^{ab},$$
where $f_{\rm extra}$ is a specified smooth force map along the state and $N_{\rm extra}^{ab}=-N_{\rm extra}^{ba}$ is a specified smooth torque map. A quadrupole convention that may be adopted is
$$f_{\rm quad}^a=-\frac16J^{bcde}\nabla^aR_{bcde},\qquad N_{\rm quad}^{ab}=\frac43R^{[a}{}_{cde}J^{b]cde},$$
with $J^{bcde}$ satisfying the algebraic symmetries of the curvature tensor, carrying units $\mathrm{kg\,m^4\,s^{-2}}$, and brackets including the factor $1/2$. Any evolved $J$ or higher moment needs its own transport or constitutive law; without it the multipole equations are not a closed initial-value model.

The pole-dipole and multipole equations are adopted finite-dimensional truncations, not derivations from the moment integrals above. Their use as approximations for a material body is restricted to regimes in which its size is small compared with the relevant curvature and background-variation lengths and omitted moment effects are negligible on the stated finite interval. These conditions are qualitative applicability assumptions here: this postulate supplies no uniform error bound, no convergence of truncations, and no global existence claim. No experimental result or measurement is asserted.

Adopt the neutral pole-dipole equations and local body moments of [[post-rpm-mpd-truncation]] and [[def-rpm-body-moments]]. Suppose a solution satisfies the TD condition $S^{ab}p_b=0$, with future timelike $p$, and remains in the local admissible region of [[lem-rpm-td-local-closure]] where $K$ is invertible and $W=K^{-1}p$ is future timelike. Then, on its local interval of existence,
$$\mu:=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}\quad\text{and}\quad \frac12S_{ab}S^{ab}$$
are constant. If the initial spin tensor is zero, it remains zero and the solution obeys
$$p=\frac{\mu}{c}U,\qquad D_\tau p=0,\qquad D_\tau U=0,$$
so the representative curve is a timelike geodesic with constant rest mass $M=\mu/c$. The claims stop if the local TD admissible region ends; no global extension follows.

Use the charged/spinning body-model conventions of the now-authored batch-24 carrier [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]: a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-+++)$, coordinates $x^0=ct$ in metres, $c>0$, and a $C^2$ future timelike representative curve $\zeta:I\to M$ parametrized by proper time $\tau$ in seconds, with $U=d\zeta/d\tau$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. The actual supplier defines these quantities and the SI electromagnetic-tensor convention used here. Assume Countable Choice for the GR smooth-structure, convex-normal and parallel-transport suppliers used below.

**(a) Flat isolated-body moments.** Choose an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and its chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ as in [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]], with the SI coordinate convention $x^0=ct$ and $x^i$ in metres of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]]. Thus $e_0$ is future unit timelike and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the positively oriented orthonormal spatial basis. Let $T$ be a $C^\infty$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field on the affine Minkowski spacetime $A$, whose chart components $T^{ab}$ are the model stress-energy densities with units $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}$. The coordinate-time image $J:=\{x^0(\zeta(\tau))/c:\tau\in I\}$ is an open interval, and $\zeta(t)$ denotes the unique point of the curve with coordinate time $t$; this is well-defined because future timelike curves have strictly increasing inertial coordinate time. For a finite closed interval $[t_1,t_2]\subset\mathbb R$, define
$$K_{[t_1,t_2]}:=\overline{\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:\text{there are }t\in[t_1,t_2]\text{ and }a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}\text{ with }T^{ab}(ct,\mathbf x)\ne0\}}.$$
Assume $K_{[t_1,t_2]}$ is compact for every such interval. For each $t\in\mathbb R$, define the spatial support by
$$\operatorname{supp}_tT:=\overline{\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3:\text{there are }a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}\text{ with }T^{ab}(ct,\mathbf x)\ne0\}}.$$
At a fixed time $t$, the spatial slice has coordinates $\mathbf x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^3$ and three-dimensional Lebesgue measure $d^3x$; define
$$p^a(t):=\frac1c\int_{\mathbb R^3}T^{0a}(ct,\mathbf x)\,d^3x,$$
and, for the representative event $\zeta(t)$ on that time slice, define
$$S_{\zeta(t)}^{ab}(t):=\frac1c\int_{\mathbb R^3}\left((x-\zeta(t))^aT^{0b}(ct,\mathbf x)-(x-\zeta(t))^bT^{0a}(ct,\mathbf x)\right)d^3x.$$
Here $(x-\zeta(t))^0=0$ on the chosen slice, $p$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, and $S_{\zeta(t)}$ has units $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. These are definitions of moments; no conservation is asserted by clause (a).

**(b) Local curved-body moments.** Let $z\in M$ and let $U_0$ be a convex normal neighborhood containing $z$. Let $\Sigma=i(S)\subset U_0$ be a $C^1$ embedded spacelike hypersurface through $z$, where $S$ is a three-dimensional $C^1$ manifold without boundary and $i:S\to U_0$ is an injective $C^1$ immersion that is a homeomorphism onto its image. Thus each tangent space $T_x\Sigma$ is three-dimensional; require the restriction of $g_x$ to it to be positive definite. Let $n_x$ be its continuous future unit normal, meaning $g_x(n_x,n_x)=-1$ and $g_x(n_x,w)=0$ for every $w\in T_x\Sigma$. For a local parametrization $X:V\subseteq\mathbb R^3\to\Sigma$, put $g^\Sigma_{ij}(y):=g_{X(y)}(\partial_iX,\partial_jX)$ and define
$$d\Sigma:=\sqrt{\det(g^\Sigma_{ij}(y))}\,dy^1dy^2dy^3.$$
The positive-definite condition makes this density positive, and the coordinate-change rule makes the resulting measure independent of the parametrization; $dy^1dy^2dy^3$ is Lebesgue measure on $V$. Let $T$ be a smooth symmetric type-$(2,0)$ stress-energy tensor field on $U_0$, with components in an orthonormal tetrad in joules per cubic metre; only its restriction $T|_\Sigma$ is used. With $(n_x)_b:=g_{bc}(x)n_x^c$, define
$$\operatorname{supp}_\Sigma(T|_\Sigma):=\overline{\{x\in\Sigma:T_x\ne0\}}^{\,\Sigma}.$$
Assume this restricted support is a compact subset of $U_0$ and that all displayed integrands are absolutely integrable with respect to $d\Sigma$. For every $x\in\Sigma$, let $v(x):=\exp_z^{-1}(x)\in T_zM$ be the unique joining position vector supplied by [[thm-gr-convex-normal-neighborhoods]] and [[thm-gr-local-geodesics-and-exponential-map]]. Let $H_{x\to z}:T_xM\to T_zM$ be parallel transport along that unique geodesic, with existence, uniqueness and metric preservation as in [[lem-gr-parallel-transport-and-geodesic-speed]]. Define $T^\sharp(n_x)^a:=T^{ab}(x)(n_x)_b$ and
$$p_z:=\frac1c\int_\Sigma H_{x\to z}\!\left(-T^\sharp(n_x)\right)d\Sigma,\qquad S_z:=\frac1c\int_\Sigma v(x)\wedge H_{x\to z}\!\left(-T^\sharp(n_x)\right)d\Sigma,$$
where $(v\wedge w)^{ab}:=v^aw^b-v^bw^a$ and the finite-dimensional vector and tensor integrals are taken componentwise in any basis of $T_zM$. The resulting $p_z$ and $S_z$ are a vector and an antisymmetric tensor at $z$; their units are $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-1}}$. “Support on $\Sigma$” here means only compact support of the restriction $T|_\Sigma$; it does not assert that the ambient smooth field $T$ has spacetime support contained in $\Sigma$.

Use SI units: coordinates are metres, proper time is seconds, $c>0$ is in metres per second, $p$ is in kilogram metres per second, $S$ is in kilogram metres squared per second, and $R$ has inverse-square-metre components. Let $z:I\to M$ be a $C^2$ future timelike worldline parametrized by proper time, with $U=dz/d\tau$ and $g(U,U)=-c^2$. $$D_\tau p^a=f^a:=-\frac12R^a{}_{bcd}U^bS^{cd},\qquad D_\tau S^{ab}=p^aU^b-p^bU^a.\tag{1}$$

Put $\mu:=\sqrt{-g(p,p)}>0$, $m:=-g(p,U)/c^2>0$, $C^a:=S^{ab}p_b$, and define the linear map

$$K^a{}_b:=\mu^2\delta^a_b-\frac12S^{ac}R_{cbde}S^{de}.$$

At every state where $K$ is invertible and $W:=K^{-1}p$ is future timelike, the TD condition $C=0$ and (1) imply

$$KU=mc^2p,\qquad U=\frac{cW}{\sqrt{-g(W,W)}}.\tag{2}$$

Conversely, on the open state region where $p$ and $W$ are future timelike and $K$ is invertible, the normalized formula for $U$ in (2), together with (1), defines a smooth local ODE. A solution initialized with $C=0$ preserves $C=0$. While it remains in that admissible region, $\mu$ and $S_{ab}S^{ab}/2$ are constant. If $S=0$, then $p=(\mu/c)U$, $D_\tau p=0$, and $D_\tau U=0$. Equations (1) are hypotheses of this mathematical lemma, not a physical derivation of a stress-energy moment model.
